newsitem.title: CANADA: Crestar Energy to acquire Grad & Walker.
newsitem.headline: Crestar Energy to acquire Grad & Walker.

text.p: Crestar Energy Inc. agreed on Wednesday to acquire Grad & Walker Energy Corp. for C$336.2 million ($244.1 million) in the latest deal in Canada's merger-happy oil patch.
Under terms of the friendly deal, Crestar would acquire Grad & Walker for C$13.50 ($9.80) a share in cash or 0.509 of a Crestar share for each Grad & Walker share.
Crestar would also assume about C$75 million ($55 million) in Grad & Walker debt.

The two Calgary-based companies, both involved in oil exploration and production in southwestern Saskatchewan and central Alberta, said holding company Grad & Walker Resources -- owned by company founders Stan Grad and Willard Walker -- would tender its 15 percent stake to the offer.
Officers and directors owning an additional 6 percent also said they would support the deal, which represented a 45 percent premium over Grad & Walker's average trading price in June.

"This is a substantial premium and clearly it allows the Grad & Walker shareholders to realize value today that might have taken some time in the market for them to achieve," Crestar Chief Executive Barry Jackson told a conference call.

Grad & Walker began operations in 1986 when Walker -- Wal-Mart Stores Inc. founder Sam Walton's first store manager -- gave Alberta rancher Grad enough Wal-Mart stock to borrow cash to start the company after the two met by chance in the southern United States.
The company went public in 1993, but soon faced a cash crunch when it acquired another small oil company with debt financing just as Canadian natural gas prices slumped.

Despite a restructuring two years ago that saw Grad & Walker emerge from the financial crisis, the firm remained out of favor with the stock market. The restructuring included the sale to Crestar of its Mantario, Saskatchewan oil field for C$46 million (34 million).

"In 1997, things were going fine but valuations hadn't caught up to us. After our troubles in '95, the market had just moved on," Grad & Walker President Brad Hurtubise said in a telephone interview. "We're cheap and when you're cheap in this kind of market, and you have the quality of assets that we have, you can't last long."
Crestar expects to drill 150 to 200 wells on the Grad & Walker lands over the next 18 months, in addition to the 60 the target firm budgeted for 1997.
Grad & Walker produces about 12,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day and has about 500,000 acres of undeveloped land, which holds the potential for more gains from exploration drilling, he said.

Jackson, whose own company is valued at almost C$2 billion ($1.5 billion), would not make financial projections for the combined companies, but analysts said the new production meant higher cash flow for Crestar.
"It's not a cheap acquisition, but it is going to improve cash flow in 1998," said Ken Faircloth, analyst with Goepel Shields & Partners.
Shares in Grad & Walker topped actives on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Wednesday, soaring C$2.35 to C$13.50. Crestar rose C$1.60 to $26.70
